_readme:
Every word the game says. Edit anything in here freely — nothing in this file is code. Two rules: keep the double quotes at the start and end of each block of text, and if you need a line break inside a paragraph use

. Text in ... comes out in the warm dawn colour. HTML attributes use single quotes on purpose so you never have to escape anything.

briefing._note: The opening, as an ordered list. Add, cut, reorder or rewrite freely — the game reads this array and nothing else. One beat must keep "kind":"naming" or the world can never be named and the game cannot start. "kind":"commission" is the screen with the name and ship fields. Everything else is "kind":"text".

beats.title: The Anchorage
beats.subtitle: Deep survey · single operator · sector CS 4

body: Nine ships. Forty thousand people, asleep. They launched before anyone had found them a destination — deliberately, so no committee could defer the programme the way the last one was deferred.
You are the part of that gamble that has to work.

beats.subtitle: Read this before you go down
body: One more thing. There was a survey here two hundred years ago. The Meridian, six crew, commanded by Ilse Vantaa. They filed a recommendation and no fleet ever came.
Their camps run west along the trail, ahead of you. So does everything else they left.

You come in low. Behind the dawn line the ground is bare and black, ninety days of ash going cold. Ahead of it, in the twilight, a strip of green two thousand kilometres long is coming up as you watch — and it will be full canopy by the time you are down, and ash again by the time you leave. Nothing here stands still long enough to be mapped twice.

There is one way into it. The herd tramples a trail west through the new growth every ninety days, and it is the only ground on this planet a person can walk. You are landing on the trail because there is nowhere else to land.
There is a light on that trail. Small, steady, and two hundred years old. Nothing in the Meridian's filed record accounts for a light.

beats.title: CS 4-9 b
beats.subtitle: Second planet · unnamed
body: Eighty-eight day rotation. Gravity 1.3 g. A habitable band three hundred kilometres wide, moving west at fifteen and a half kilometres an hour, forever.
beats.hint: This is the name the fleet will read.

soil.name: Soil chemistry
soil.finding: Ash-derived, and freshly — this ground burns to nothing every ninety days and comes back. Mineral-rich, poor in fixed nitrogen. Crops would need help for a generation and then they would not.

water.name: Surface water
water.finding: Meltwater, low salinity, drinkable after filtration. It runs for a day in ninety and then it is ice again.

rad.name: Radiation
rad.finding: Magnetosphere weak but sufficient. Surface dose survivable unshielded; a roof solves the rest.

bio.name: Biosphere
bio.finding: Six tonnes each, walking. No stomach flora hostile to us, no airborne prion analogue. We could live alongside this.

site.name: Settlement site
site.finding: A clearing, sheltered, with a floor that holds water eleven days after each dawn. If it is anywhere, it is here.

season.name: Seasonal extremes
season.finding: The night side reaches sixty below and holds it for weeks. Anything we build has to be able to walk, or to sleep.

c1.name: Camp one
c1.title: Camp one — Meridian, day 41
c1.body:
Marker one, logged 41:06:22 local, all six present and well.

We are calling the planet nothing yet — Vantaa says naming it before the survey is finished is bad discipline, and she is right, and everyone has a name for it anyway.

The band is generous. We can live here. I want that in the record plainly before I start qualifying it in the report.

Soil series complete and filed. Ash-derived, mineral-rich, poor in fixed nitrogen. A generation of work and then none.

— T. Ruiz, for the commander
c1.gift: Ruiz's soil series, complete, two hundred years before you got here.

reveals.note: Wrote the early logs. Meticulous timekeeping, to the second.
Commanded the Meridian survey. Six crew, no relief, no return.

c2.name: Camp two
c2.title: Camp two — Meridian, day 1,205
c2.body:
Third move. We have the rhythm of it: strike at hour six, walk until the growth thins, make camp in the green again.

Ruiz took the sledge past the dawn line to the frost and brought back numbers nobody wanted. Sixty below on the night side and it holds for weeks. Whatever gets built here has to be able to move, or to sleep through it.

Okonkwo has not slept properly since planetfall. She says the light does not change enough to tell her body anything, and that she has started to find the fixed sun difficult to be under. Lindqvist has her on a schedule and a lamp. It is not working yet.

— T. Ruiz
c2.gift: Ruiz's cold-side telemetry, taken past the line at some cost.

reveals.note: Biologist. Stopped being able to sleep almost immediately. The light never changes here.
Physician. Also ran the relay — six people, everyone doubled up.

c3.name: Camp three
c3.title: Camp three — Meridian, day 2,940
c3.body:
Earth acknowledged.

That is the word. Acknowledged. Recommendation received and filed. Colony programme deferred pending review. Review to be scheduled.

Vantaa read it to all of us standing up, in full, twice, and then said we would continue the survey, because the survey is what we are for. Nobody argued. Nobody said anything at all.

Radiation series finished and filed with the rest of it. Demir has kept the reactor inside tolerance four years past its rating and does not talk about how.

— T. Ruiz
c3.gift: The radiation series — filed, complete, and read by no one.

reveals.note: Engineer. Kept a reactor alive years past its rating.

c4.name: Camp four
c4.title: Camp four — Meridian, day 4,860 (?)
c4.body:
[ transcription note: hand unsteady from here on. dates internally inconsistent — this entry is logged as day 4,860 and also as day 4,680. ]

We have moved this camp eleven times and not at all in nineteen years.

Ruiz worked out that where the canopy closes over completely the burn goes across the top of it and the ground underneath never catches, and once you know a thing like that you cannot un-know it. We walked to the thickest of it and stopped. Then further in. The growth is thin under a roof like that and the light never really changes and nobody has proposed going back.

Raman is drawing again, which is good. She has drawn the clearing below the camp eleven times this month. They are all slightly different and she says they are all correct.

Hydrology closed out. It was closed out a long time ago.

— I. Vantaa
c4.gift: The hydrology record, closed out and left where someone might find it.

reveals.note: Cartographer. Drew the same valley eleven times in a month and said each was correct.

c5.name: Camp five
c5.title: Camp five — Meridian, final entry
c5.body:
I am the last one and I have stopped pretending the survey continues.

Something I never put in a report: the ashwaiters do not migrate. They burrow in behind the herd and wait out the whole ninety days in the dark, and when the growth comes round again they are exactly where they were. I used to think that was a horror. I have come to think it is the only honest way to live here, and I am aware of what that says about me.

We found a world. It was a good world. That part we did correctly.

If you are reading this then someone came after all, and you are standing in my camp with a survey of your own to finish. Do not do what I did. Send it, and then keep walking.

— Ilse Vantaa

reveals.note: Wrote a final entry stating she was the last of the six alive.

g1.title: A. OKONKWO
g1.label: year 9
g1.body:
A cairn with a plate cut from hull stock. The lettering is careful and even.

She stopped being able to sleep in the light.
g1.reveal: Died in year nine. The first.

g2.title: Y. DEMIR
g2.label: year 17
g2.body:
Hull plate again, same hand, less even now.

He kept the reactor running four years past its rating.

g3.title: P. RAMAN
g3.label: year 24
g3.body:
The lettering has gone irregular, the spacing wrong, as though cut by someone working from memory of how letters go.

She drew everything. At the end she drew the same clearing eleven times.

g4.title: T. RUIZ
g4.label: year 31
g4.body:
Barely legible. Cut slowly, and by someone who had to stop and start.

He said the numbers were fine.
g4.reveal: Died in year thirty-one. His last telemetry is unusable, and he filed it as sound.

g5.title: I. VANTAA
g5.label: year 41
g5.body:
Hull plate, cut clean and square and level — the steadiest hand of any marker on this planet, and not the hand that cut the others.

She was right about the world.

Vantaa's last entry says she was the last of the six alive. Someone buried her.
g5.reveal: Buried by a steady hand, after writing that she was the last one alive.

shelter.name: Unlogged camp
shelter.title: Unlogged camp — no designation
shelter.body:
One shelter, out past the last of the growth, on ground that has not been warm in a hundred and eighty years. It is not on any Meridian manifest.

There is a relay terminal inside, still under power, and a single record left open on it.

confession.title: M. Lindqvist — personal record, undated
confession.body:
I was the physician and I ran the relay, because there were six of us and everyone did two jobs.

I had the medical series before anyone. Okonkwo first, then all of us: sleep architecture coming apart, circadian phase running free, and after the first decade something worse and slower underneath it. Ninety-day light. Our biology has no answer to it and neither did I. It does not kill you. It takes you apart over thirty years and you are the last to notice, and by the time you would notice you are not the one doing the noticing.

I was holding the survey recommendation for transmission on day 2,900. Six lives on one side. Forty thousand on the other, asleep, with no fuel to go anywhere else once they were pointed here.

I changed one word. The recommendation went out as withdrawn.

Then I wrote the reply myself, because it would take nineteen years to arrive and I could not have Ilse reading the real one. Deferred pending review. She believed in that committee for the rest of her life. She died angry at an office that had never received anything to be angry about.

I buried them all. I have been alone eleven years now and I am, as far as I can tell, still myself, which I no longer trust as evidence of anything.

If you are reading this you are a surveyor and you have your own recommendation to send, and you have just found out that the world is good and that it will take your people apart slowly and they will not notice.

I am not going to tell you what to do. I have already found out what it costs to decide that for other people.

— M. Lindqvist
confession.reveal: Altered the Meridian recommendation to withdrawn, and forged the reply. Buried the other five. Reason: the ninety-day light takes human beings apart over thirty years, and nobody notices it happening.

shelter.afterReadToast: Your six findings say yes. Their forty years say yes, and in thirty years you will not be yourselves. Press T when you know what to send.

fleetTransmission._DO_NOT_EDIT_THIS_NOTE: This block is the placeholder. It is the one part of the game that is not to be written, polished, or expanded by anyone but the author. The marker line below stays until she replaces the whole block herself.
fleetTransmission.kicker: Received · Anchorage relay · delayed 6 y 4 m
fleetTransmission.subtitle: Recorded before cold sleep
fleetTransmission.marker: [ Placeholder. Replace this whole block — it is the one part that cannot be generated. ]
body: I'm told this reaches you years after I record it, and that by then I'll have been asleep for most of them. I don't understand the arithmetic and I've decided not to.
Take your time out there. I know you can't. I'm saying it anyway.
Find us somewhere with weather.

prompt.title: What do you send?
prompt.subtitle: One transmission · six years in flight · no revision
body: Your findings say the world is good, and they are not wrong. Lindqvist's medical series says it will take your people apart over thirty years and they will not notice it happening.
The fleet has no fuel to go anywhere else. Whatever you send, they are coming here or they are coming to nothing.
prompt.hint: The last surveyor who stood here chose the third one.

clean.heading: Recommendation transmitted
body: The recommendation goes out clean. They come, and the landing is good, and the first decade is the best decade any of them have had.

In year thirty-one a physician in the settlement notices that the sleep records have been drifting for a long time, and pulls the old survey, and finds that the answer was on this planet the whole time, filed in an unlogged shelter north of everything, by someone who had worked it out two centuries early and had no way to make anyone believe her.
They live. It costs them something they never agreed to.

caveat.heading: Recommendation transmitted
body: The recommendation goes out with the medical series attached and a sentence you write yourself, which is that the world is good and it will cost them something slow.

They come. They have six years in flight to plan for it, and they use them. They build below ground and they rotate crews into shielded sleep on a schedule that a physician two hundred years dead worked out and never got to send. The first generation is hard. The second one is born to it, and the drift is smaller in them, and smaller again after that.
The name you gave that clearing is the name on the charts, and the settlement carries hers.

withdraw.heading: Withdrawal transmitted
body: The withdrawal reaches the relay in six years. The Anchorage holds its heading because it has no other heading to hold, and passes {planet} at four hundred million kilometres without slowing.
Nobody aboard wakes up. That is the mercy in it, and it is the only one.
Mara Lindqvist made this decision alone, on worse information, and spent eleven years afterwards deciding whether she had been right. You had her notes and you made it in a minute.

summary.neverFoundSixth: You never found out what happened to the sixth.
summary.sliceNote: Slice ends here. In the full game this is world one of four, and she is aboard.

failure.title: Survey terminated
failure.water: Water gone. The band moved on without you, the way it moves on without everything.
failure.coda: The fleet is still coming. It does not know yet.
